summary: At Year 3, 'angle' is a dual idea: the static corner of a shape AND the dynamic amount of turn/opening between two lines meeting at a point. The central hurdle is separating the SIZE of an angle (its opening/turn) from the LENGTH of the lines forming it — children default to judging by side length. Guidance develops the dynamic turn/opening conception first through embodied turning and 'opening' objects, deliberately varies arm length against a fixed opening to confront the length misconception, then binds turn and corner together explicitly.
misconceptions: An angle is bigger when its arms/sides are longer — size judged by line length rather than opening (Askew & Wiliam; Xu et al. length-inconsistent trials near 0%)
An angle is 'the distance between the ends of the lines' — a gap between the tips rather than the opening
The whole-object assumption: 'angle' refers to the entire figure, so the amount-of-turn dimension is never separated out (van Hiele holistic processing)
A corner and a turn are unrelated ideas — the child fails to see a shape's corner as a turn, or a turn as producing a corner

activities.title: Turn, then open: building angle as amount of turn
steps: Physically turn your whole body a quarter turn, then a half turn; then do the same with an arm held out, describing each turn aloud.
Open a book, a pair of scissors, or a fan slowly and watch the angle between the parts grow while the two parts themselves stay exactly the same length.
Hold two hinged strips (geo-strips or a split-pin angle maker) pinned at one point; swing one strip open from a small opening to a large one and describe what is changing.
State in your own words what you actually had to do to 'make the angle bigger' (open the lines further apart / turn more).
activities.insight: An angle is the amount of turn or opening between two lines meeting at a point — something you grow by opening the lines apart, not by making the lines longer.

activities.title: Change the arms, keep the opening: confronting the length rule
steps: Set a hinged angle maker to a fixed opening. Predict aloud whether making both arms twice as long would make the angle bigger, and say why BEFORE testing.
Lengthen (or swap for longer strips) both arms while keeping the opening unchanged; check whether the opening/turn has changed.
Reverse it: hold the arm length fixed and only change the opening, describing which action actually changes the angle.

Compare two drawn angles with the SAME opening but very different arm lengths: predict which is bigger, then overlay them vertex-on-vertex with one arm aligned so the second arms fall exactly on top of each other.
activities.insight: Making the lines longer does not make the angle bigger; only changing the opening/turn changes the angle. Length of the arms and size of the angle are independent.

activities.title: Walking the shape: a corner is a turn
steps: Walk the perimeter of a large taped square or rectangle, making the turn at each corner and feeling that each turn is a quarter turn.
At each corner, stop and point to the corner where you turned, then mark the arc inside the corner between the two sides, noticing that this square corner and your turn are both a quarter turn.
Place a hinged angle maker onto the corner of a familiar 2-D shape so its arms lie along the two sides; describe the corner as an amount of turn.

Say how much turn a square corner is (a quarter turn), then use the hinge on a narrower (sharper) and a wider corner to say whether each corner is less or more than a quarter turn of one side onto the other.
activities.insight: A shape's corner is an angle: it is the amount one side would turn about the corner point to lie along the other side, which a hinge laid on the corner can show. At a square or rectangle corner this is a quarter turn, the same as the quarter turn you make walking round it, which links the static and dynamic meanings of 'angle'.

activities.title: A fresh name for the opening (optional scaffold)
steps: Agree a fresh, non-length word for the quantity being measured (the 'opening' or 'turn amount') and use it instead of 'angle' for a while.
Each time you compare two angles, point to the opening/turn with the new name while varying arm length, tip distance, or figure size, checking only the opening decides.
Return to the word 'angle' once you can consistently point to the opening as the thing being compared.
activities.insight: Giving the measured quantity a fresh, non-length name may help stop 'angle' being mapped onto the whole figure, so the size dimension (the opening/turn) can be separated out.

activities.title: Check and discriminate: same opening, different arms
steps: Judge several angle pairs with varied arm lengths — some pairs with EQUAL openings and some with GENUINELY DIFFERENT openings — choosing 'same', 'bigger', or 'smaller' for each, so that each choice is sometimes the correct answer.

For each judgement, state the REASON before confirming — e.g. 'same, because the lines have opened by the same amount', or 'that one is bigger because it has turned further open' — justifying by the opening/turn, not the arm length.
Explain whether two lines that meet but barely open apart make a big or a small angle, and why.
activities.insight: You can reliably decide whether an angle is the same, bigger or smaller by comparing openings/turns, ignoring arm length and tip distance, and you can say why.

checkQuestion: Put in front of the child two angles with the SAME opening, one drawn with long lines and one with short lines. Ask: 'Which angle is bigger — the one with the long lines, the one with the short lines, or are they the same?' Then, whatever they answer: 'Now tell me how you know.'
checkAnswer: They are the same size, because an angle is how much the lines have turned or opened apart from each other, and both have opened by the same amount — the length of the lines does not change the angle.
